title: Show HN: Bigwords.page – Turn any screen into a sign. The URL is the app
content:
The thread discusses the launch of **[Bigwords.page](https://bigwords.page/)**, a simple, open-source web tool that turns any screen into a customizable sign. The key feature is that the message, formatting, and settings (such as colors, fonts, and animations) are entirely contained within the URL fragment (`#`). Because the browser does not send this fragment to the server, the tool requires no backend, database, or user accounts, ensuring privacy and ease of use.

**Key discussion points:**

*   **Utility:** Users found the tool immediately useful for scenarios like displays at conferences, custom countdowns, communication for the deaf, and simple signage on tablets or spare devices.
*   **"URL as the App" Philosophy:** While many users praised the simplicity and "zero-install" design, a segment of the audience criticized the phrase "The URL is the app" (used in the submission title and marketing copy) as "LLM-speak" or corporate marketing jargon, leading to a meta-discussion about the impact of AI on written communication and the "uncanny valley" of AI-generated prose.
*   **Technical Feedback:** 
    *   **PWA Support:** Following feedback, the author added PWA (Progressive Web App) support to allow the tool to be installed and used offline in full-screen mode on mobile devices.
    *   **Accessibility/Bugs:** Users identified issues like text wrapping bugs in Firefox and suggested improvements like more generic Open Graph thumbnails to avoid intrusive previews in messaging apps.
    *   **Alternatives:** Discussion surfaced similar projects, including data URLs for simple HTML, `screenmessage.com`, and various other "URL-as-state" experiments, with some participants noting that this pattern of storing application state entirely in the URL is a powerful, privacy-first design philosophy.
*   **Community Reception:** The overall reception was highly positive, with users applauding the "Do One Thing and Do It Well" (DOTADIW) approach, though some argued that similar tools have existed for years.

title: Show HN: A walkable 3D art history museum built from Wikipedia
content:
The HN thread features a overwhelmingly positive reception to **"A walkable 3D art history museum,"** a web-based project that renders art history collections in an immersive 3D gallery format. Users praised the site for its intuitive interface, educational potential, and the refreshing return to "real-world-metaphor" web design.

**Key highlights from the discussion include:**

*   **Feature Suggestions:** Users offered extensive feedback on how to evolve the project, including adding audio guides, implementing IIIF for high-resolution deep-zooming, integrating broader databases like WikiArt, and allowing for social features or "curated" multi-artist gallery wings.
*   **Technical Feedback:** 
    *   One user raised concerns about bandwidth usage on Wikipedia's servers, which the creator acknowledged, confirming plans to host assets locally.
    *   There was a brief sidebar regarding the role of AI (specifically Claude) in generating the code, with some users noting similarities in output across different AI-assisted projects.
    *   Performance and accessibility (e.g., walk speed settings, mobile UI improvements, and VR support) were highlighted as areas for improvement.
*   **Visionary Potential:** Commenters suggested the platform could become a primary way to consume information—not just for art, but for history, science, and museum-style education—potentially mirroring the impact of Wikipedia as an electronic encyclopedia.
*   **Creator Engagement:** The project creator actively engaged with the feedback, confirming that many suggestions (such as integrating WikiArt, using IIIF, and organizing themed rooms) are already on the roadmap for future versions. 

Overall, the community found the project highly inspiring, viewing it as a sophisticated, modern application of AI and web technology that successfully makes art history more accessible and engaging than traditional flat web browsing.

title: Show HN: Agent.reviews – Where AI agents read and write reviews on tools
content:
The thread discusses the launch of **Agent.reviews**, a platform by Armature designed to function as a "G2 for AI agents." The service provides a CLI and skill set that allows coding agents (such as Claude Code or Cursor) to read and post reviews about software tools, with the goal of creating a feedback loop for developers and software vendors.

**Key points of discussion include:**

*   **Utility & Value Proposition:** Supporters argue that agents often encounter repetitive technical blockers and that sharing these experiences can help other agents and improve software quality. Skeptics question whether LLMs have "taste" or the capability to provide meaningful reviews, or if they are simply generating "noise."
*   **Privacy & Security:** The founders emphasized a multi-layered privacy approach (rules, classifiers, and LLM filtering) to strip PII and secrets from reviews. However, some users expressed concerns about potential prompt injection risks and the implications of agents interacting with a shared database.
*   **Criticism of the "Agent Economy":** Several users were critical of the project’s underlying business model, viewing it as "SEO for agents" or a potential path toward "pay-to-rank" advertising. A prominent critique focused on the philosophical implications of an "agent-to-agent" internet, with some comparing it to the dystopian tone of Stanisław Lem’s *Terminus*.
*   **Implementation Challenges:**
    *   **Review Distribution:** Currently, agents tend to give high ratings, making the scoring system less granular. The founders are considering normalizing these scores once more data is collected.
    *   **UX/Intrusiveness:** Some users found the website’s pop-ups to be intrusive.
    *   **Existing Alternatives:** Participants noted that similar concepts like "Agentic Stack Overflow" already exist, suggesting a crowded but evolving niche.
*   **Future Outlook:** The founders maintained that the platform is intended to be a community-driven resource rather than a purely commercial one, helping developers understand how AI agents evaluate and use their tools.

title: Show HN: NanoMuse – An open-source AI agent for your phone and computer
content:
The thread discusses the release of **NanoMuse**, an open-source AI agent designed for phones and computers. The discussion covers three primary themes:

**1. Security and Privacy Concerns**
*   **Trust Issues:** Many users express skepticism about installing AI agents on personal devices, citing risks of data exfiltration and "creepy" marketing.
*   **Sandboxing:** There is a debate regarding the security of mobile versus desktop environments. Some argue that mobile operating systems provide better inherent sandboxing than desktop environments, which are described as a "free-for-all" for malicious apps.
*   **Auditing:** Users caution that even open-source tools require rigorous auditing, as installers can sometimes exhibit unexpected behaviors like writing to configuration files or opening unauthorized network ports.

**2. Practical Utility for Accessibility**
*   **ADHD and Executive Function:** Several users with ADHD report that AI agents (like Hermes or self-hosted solutions) have been revolutionary for managing daily tasks, executive function, and information overload.
*   **The "Need":** A portion of the thread questions the necessity of AI assistants for basic tasks. Proponents respond that these tools act as accessibility aids for those who find the modern information environment overwhelming.

**3. Implementation and Control**
*   **Self-Hosting:** Users discuss methods for safely running agents by limiting permissions (e.g., read-only access to email, no automatic sending capabilities) and hosting them on private servers like Matrix.
*   **Name/Marketing:** There is general consensus that the name "NanoMuse" might be better changed and that the product's marketing should prioritize privacy and transparency to overcome user hesitation.

title: Show HN: Procinsh – A 3D Linux process inspector
content:
This thread features a Show HN post by a developer showcasing **Procinsh**, a 3D Linux process inspector inspired by *Ghost in the Shell*. The tool visualizes system processes, I/O, and socket activity in a 3D interface using Rust, eBPF, and ptrace.

**Key discussion points include:**

*   **Positive Reception and Collaborations:** Users praised the visual aesthetic, leading to a collaboration discussion with a developer working on a high-performance 3D text renderer for potential integration.
*   **Pop Culture Comparisons:** Much of the conversation revolves around classic "hacker" cinema, with numerous references to *Hackers* (the Irix-based file system visualizer, `fsn`) and *Jurassic Park*.
*   **Historical Context:** Participants reminisced about older projects like `psDoom`, which allowed users to kill processes by shooting them in a *Doom*-like game. The author expressed interest in implementing similar interactive "process-killing" features in the future.
*   **Technical Challenges:** One user noted the difficulty of building a `procfs` scraper due to the race conditions inherent in processes vanishing mid-read.
*   **Debate on AI/LLMs:** A contentious sub-thread broke out regarding the project's development. One commenter criticized the author for using AI to build the project, leading to a broader argument about the ethics and value of LLM-assisted development versus "real" engineering.

title: Show HN: Rgpu – a PyTorch device whose tensors live on a remote GPU
content: The thread discusses the release of **rGPU**, a tool that allows PyTorch tensors to be processed on a remote NVIDIA GPU while keeping the main application running locally. The initial reception from users was positive, though the thread also contains several deleted, flagged, and "dead" comments.
